I recently started formalizing the qubit, but fairly quickly noticed that I was beginning to define things such as density operators, states, observables, etc. These are obviously concepts that should be defined once through a general finite-dimensional quantum-system API rather than specifically for qubits.

QuantumInfo already contains a lot of the relevant mathematics, but it was developed somewhat independently from the rest of Physlib and is mostly formulated in terms of matrices indexed by a Fintype. I was therefore a little hesitant to build new Physlib developments directly on top of it. At the same time, there seem to be several places in Physlib that have already started moving in this direction independently (QuantumSystem, FiniteTarget, and some TODOs around integrating QuantumInfo).

Rather than adding yet another local version of these definitions, I tried to lay out a possible roadmap for a common API 1525 and defined the first operators 1526.

The starting point would be the existing FiniteHilbertSpace d (𝓗[d]). On a finite-dimensional Hilbert space H, consider the algebra of operators

𝒜(H) := H →L[ℂ] H.

Mathlib already gives this the structure of a C*-algebra. After choosing a basis, this is equivalent to Matrix d d ℂ, so the existing matrix-based results in QuantumInfo should be reusable rather than reimplemented.

The rough hierarchy I have in mind is

𝒜(H) ⊃ Observable H ⊃ 𝒜(H)₊ ⊃ State H, Effect H.

The self-adjoint operators in 𝒜(H) are the observables. Positivity then gives the natural order on these operators. A state is represented by a positive operator with trace one, while an effect is an operator between zero and the identity and represents a possible measurement outcome. A POVM collects such effects into a measurement by requiring that they sum to the identity.

Unitary conjugation A ↦ U A U† acts naturally on this whole structure, preserving observables, positivity, states, effects and the trace. This gives a common foundation for symmetries and time evolution, with self-adjoint Hamiltonians generating one-parameter unitary groups.

On top of this basic structure, one can collect the standard finite-dimensional results such as spectral decomposition, functional calculus, pure states, expectation values and entropy. It should also provide a natural foundation for composite systems, where tensor products lead to partial traces, quantum channels and general measurements.

The intention is not to reimplement the existing QuantumInfo theory, but to put a Hilbert-space/operator-algebra API underneath it and reuse the matrix results through the finite-dimensional equivalence wherever possible.

This is very much a v0.1 and intended as an open discussion rather than a settled design. I noticed that quite a few files have already started tackling pieces of this problem, so I hope we can converge on a clear path before more parallel APIs accumulate. Critique, corrections and improvements to this roadmap are very welcome.
I think this road map is really nice! I added some comments to the roadmap PR!

I’ve been thinking about what a useful general notion of a quantum system in Physlib could look like beyond the finite-dimensional setting.

A fairly clean operator-algebraic picture seems to be to take a C*-algebra A as the algebra of bounded observables. States are positive normalized linear functionals on A, while time evolution is a one-parameter group of *-automorphisms of A. This gives intrinsic notions of observables, states, mixtures, effects, symmetries and dynamics without immediately committing to a particular Hilbert-space realization.

A concrete realization is then a *-representation of A as bounded operators on some Hilbert space H. Conversely, given a state on A, the GNS construction produces such a Hilbert-space representation together with a distinguished cyclic vector reproducing the state through expectation values. So the abstract observable algebra and its states can be separated cleanly from a particular Hilbert-space realization.

One place where this seems genuinely useful is infinite systems. Instead of trying to define an infinite tensor product of Hilbert spaces, one can start with the observable algebra A_Λ of every finite subsystem Λ. Whenever Λ is contained in Γ, A_Λ embeds into A_Γ by tensoring with the identity. The infinite system can then be obtained as the C*-completion/inductive limit of these local algebras.

A state on the resulting algebra describes a compatible family of states on all finite subsystems. Choosing such a state then gives a Hilbert-space realization through GNS. This seems considerably cleaner than trying to construct an infinite tensor-product Hilbert space from the outset.

For something like hydrogen the role of the C*-algebra is somewhat different. We can again have an algebra A of bounded observables together with a representation on L²(R³), but the physical Hamiltonian

H = -ℏ²/(2m) Δ - κ/r

is unbounded and therefore is not itself an element of A. After constructing H as a self-adjoint operator, however, its time evolution U(t) = exp(-itH) is bounded and acts on the observable algebra by conjugation. This realizes the abstract time evolution of A in the chosen Hilbert-space representation.

So the same abstract framework can cover both a particle system such as hydrogen, where the dynamics is implemented by an unbounded Hamiltonian in a concrete representation, and an infinite local system, where the global dynamics may instead be obtained directly as a limit of finite-volume dynamics without there being a canonical global Hamiltonian.

This does not make the difficult analysis of hydrogen disappear. One still has to define the differential operator properly, prove self-adjointness, and ultimately needs unbounded functional/spectral calculus to construct exp(-itH), spectral projections and eigenspaces. The C*-algebraic formulation seems useful as a common outer structure for observables, states, representations and dynamics, rather than as a way of avoiding unbounded operator theory.

So roughly I am imagining three layers:

  • a general C*-algebraic quantum-system API for observables, states and dynamics,
  • Hilbert-space representations connecting the abstract system to concrete operators,
  • a separate analytic layer for unbounded Hamiltonians and spectral theory.

Does this seem like a sensible boundary, particularly with infinite/local systems in mind?

This, I think is something we will no-doubt want in Physlib. Since it seems to be useful even outside of quantum mechanics. Also it seems to compliment nicely what we already have (@Gregory Loges may be able to confirm/deny this).

Would the idea be to define a structure or a class called OperatorAlgebra and define things around that?

(Also this seems like a nice reference which might be worth linking to: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.10151)

This all sounds like a good idea - currently a lot of the operator machinery in physlib is simply tacked onto LinearPMap.
Mathlib already has CStarAlgebra, CompletelyPositiveMap, the GNS construction &c, so is the idea for the "first layer" to have physlib alii of these (e.g. with more "familiar" names) which can then more easily be integrated into the operator/analytic layers?

I've spent a fair bit of time on this for my own repo, and I'd flag reusing the matrix results through the finite-dimensional equivalence:

Mathlib's C* structure sits on the CStarMatrix synonym, not Matrix, and the CFC order lemmas don't resolve through it, NonnegSpectrumClass ℝ (CStarMatrix n n ℂ) is provable as a term but isn't found by synthesis inside CFC.rpow.

PR #39734 works around it with shortcut instances, but has been a draft since May.

I hit this building a basis indexed finite-dimensional QM repo, Happy to point you how I solved it if you'd like.

Yes its great that all of this already exists in Mathlib.
I have already started with formalizing/transferring this for our purposes.
My plan right now is to formalize the Qubit and the classical harmonic Oscillator with this language which then should give feedback on how the general structure should look like.
Once I have finished this I will have generated quite some files. Should this first go into PhyslibAlpha?
Im sure Zayn is correct in saying that making the functional calculus easy to use requires some thought and I wont get right on the first try.
Do you have any suggestions on how this iterative refinement process should be organized?

I think there are two ways to approach this:

  1. Go quickly in PhyslibAlpha, to find what works best, refine etc, whilst keeping it visible and usable for others to build on. Then refactor until something emerges which is stable, and of good quality etc. Then it should be fairly straightforward to upstream to Physlib (although still with small PRs).
  2. Go slowly and make small PRs to Physlib, with everything carefully checked and reviewed so less refinement is needed later on.

Though even in the case of 2. one should not be scared to refactor - if something goes into Physlib, and there turns out to be a better way of doing things, we can (and should) go back and modify it.

Either approach is valid, and it is really up to you. I think setting up the roadmap as you have started also really helps.

I have thought about this some more and came to realize that CStarAlgebras are quite the central structure to physics in general. I made some document to convince myself and hopefully others that this is very much needed.
If anybody has ideas or thinks there are things I have forgotten or are just plain wrong Im happy to hear about them. And Im sure there will be lots of unexpected implementation details to come. The good thing is that most of the math is already formalized.

PHYSICAL_SYSTEMS_OPERATOR_ALGEBRA.pdf

I think this centrality rises the question, where is it best to put this within Physlib. I've seen in your most recent PR that you have put it in ./Mathematics, but I don't think that is the best place for this long term. If we think it is going to be used most in QuantumMechanics, then I think it might be better for now to put it in ./QuantumMechanics.

Hi Tom, interesting read. Section 11 was the most useful bit for me, the chain from automorphism group up to channel with each one being the next plus one extra constraint, I hadn't seen it set out like that before.

I also checked your Mathlib refs and they hold up, GNS is in Analysis/CStarAlgebra/GelfandNaimarkSegal.lean and CompletelyPositiveMap.lean is there and you're right that there's no one-parameter semigroup theory.

One thing I'd settle early is where the concrete examples actually live: You said the qubit and the harmonic oscillator are next, The qubit is Matrix 2 2 ℂ, and Matrix n n ℂ isn't a CStarAlgebra at its default instances that structure sits on the CStarMatrix synonym.

You're right that B(H) carries the instance already so if the examples stay there you sidestep the whole thing. If they go into Matrix you'll hit it more or less immediately. It's not theoretical, I ran into it doing my repo log transports across the star algebra equivalence fine but rpow doesn't, NonnegSpectrumClass and Pow don't resolve through the discrimination tree.

I wrote up what transported and what didn't in the header here for my reference later: https://github.com/zblore/csd-lean4/blob/main/CsdLean4/Mathlib/Analysis/Matrix/OperatorConvexBridge.lean.

Anyway, hope it helps.

Hi Everyone. I've started a similar discussion some time ago in another thread. We didn't really come to a conclusion (and then I was offline for family holidays).

In the meantime, I did think about the problem a bit more, and had one-to-one discussions with a number of colleagues (including @Frédéric Dupuis, @Thomas Vidick , @Zoltan Zimboras , @Mirko arienzo ). People seem to agree that there is a technical problem ("what's the right level of abstraction for a general quantum API?") and a sociological problem ("how can one get a critical mass of the community to agree on it?") that are both open and important.

On the technical side:

Over the summer, @Paradoxy ported parts of our QCLib library from matrices to bounded linear operators between Hilbert spaces, and I wrote a file that at least defines trace class operators in quite some generality (though there's basically 0 API at this point). (Neither is public atm, but both could be cleaned up for publication with not too much effort).

Next on may agenda:

  • Finish my trace class operator implementation. Define functions from positive trace class operators to positive linear functionals on bounded operators. One can then also define a function to density matrices, for the special case of finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces with preferred basis. This would connect the concrete notions of "state" (as used in e.g. in Lean QuantumInfo) to the axiomatic one.
  • Have a look at POVMs. Interestingly, they need a bit more structure than a C^* algebra, as the completeness relation is stated w.r.t. the weak topology. This becomes essential if one wants to support POVMs with infinitely many outcomes. These are important in many applications: Consider e.g. the Hussimi function in quantum optics, or phase-covariant cloners of qubit states. I guess this means that ideally, POVMs should be defined for W^* algebras. Though there's currently almost no API for these in Mathlib, so maybe for the time being, one would have to define them using a concrete Hilbert space.

If anybody has comments / wants to join in, please let me know!

(So far I've hand-coded everything. I guess that was a sign for quality, like, three months ago, but maybe now it mainly means that I'm much slower than I should be?)

The "sociological problem" -- how can one get the community to agree on one standard, so that code duplication is minimized -- remains wide open, as far as I can see. Maybe we should have an online workshop?

For what it's worth, everything I have is finite dimensional and deliberately so as that is what i'm interested in. That makes the completeness relation a finite sum, so the weak topology question never arises and solves a lot of problems tbh.

On the concrete Hilbert space route it went further than I expected in that Naimark dilation is generic over POVM N ι, and Busch's Gleason type theorem is proved rather than assumed.
Where I ran into trouble was underneath, where the abstract structure meets matrices, so Matrix n n ℂ is not a CStarAlgebra at its default instances, that sits on the CStarMatrix synonym, and the transport is uneven. log moves across the star algebra equivalence cleanly, rpow does not, because NonnegSpectrumClass and Pow do not resolve through the discrimination tree.

The obvious limitation is that none of it reaches infinitely many outcomes, so your Husimi and cloner examples are outside what I have.
@David Gross Would be interested if you had any input on what @Tom Diem is planning for general operator algebras? Would be good to get this right from the start.

I had a look at @Tom Diem's plans (for QM) and his recent PR.

Mathematically, I think the direction he proposes is the right one! The common feature of any system that would count as "quantum" is that it's described by an observable algebra. States are normalized positive linear maps into the complex numbers. Etc.

So I think that this should be the foundation of a common language for quantum information, standard QM, and QFT.

However, from a "software engineering" point of view, I would like to put up for discussion an approach that differs from the way @Tom Diem's material is implemented:

Indeed, many of the definitions / results seem stated in a way that only covers the main intended use case ("a StarOrdered C^*-algebra"), even if they make sense much more broadly. That contrasts with Mathlib's successful approach of aiming for maximal reasonably generality.

Let me explain what I have in mind, using the concept of a "state". (I've written an alternative implementation covering this).

In Physlib, State is currently defined as a structure that bundles a PositiveLinearMap with a proof of unitality (f 1 = 1). It takes a CStarAlgebra and a StarOrderedRing instance as arguments, so it is restricted only to this narrow use case.

But the mathematical structure "a unital positive linear map" makes sense much more broadly. I'd suggest to define

/-- A positive linear map that preserves `1`. -/
structure UnitalPositiveLinearMap (R E₁ E₂ : Type*) [Semiring R]
    [AddCommMonoid E₁] [PartialOrder E₁] [AddCommMonoid E₂] [PartialOrder E₂]
    [Module R E₁] [Module R E₂] [One E₁] [One E₂] extends E₁ →ₚ[R] E₂, OneHom E₁ E₂

In my RFC implementation, I took @Frédéric Dupuis 's PositiveLinearMap file, and adapted it for unital maps.

Advantages I see in this approach:

  • UnitalPositiveLinearMap now has a decent API, because the Mathlib maintainers already thought about what is necessary to work with PositiveLinearMaps, and we can reuse their experience.
  • The file is written in a Mathlib-compatible way, so it may have a chance of getting merged, which would reduce the amount of divergence between Physlib and Mathlib.
  • General UnitalPositiveLinearMaps feature in many areas of QM and related fields. Examples are the time-reversal channel, or states in (General Probabilistic Theories)[https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.07469]. So we'd need such a concept sooner or later anyway.

Disadvantage:

  • More code to write.
There's a bit more in my RFC. E.g. @Tom Diem 's exepectation seem to be a special case of the general fact that the restriction of a positive linear map to a subspace is again a positive linear map.

I'd really like to hear people's opinions on this approach.

Concretely, how would you feel about this approach for unifying Physlib and QuantumInfo:

  • Grow the mathematical basics of QM in a new folder (QuantumMechanics.Basic?)
  • Use the general language as per @Tom Diem, but aim for Mathlib-style generality, quality, and idioms as per the example.
  • Let the rest of Physlib.QuantumMechanics and QuantumInfo evolve independently for the time being. If the Basic program turns out to be successful, start porting results incrementally to this general language.

I can't give a solid opinion because I'm not very familiar with the foundations of QM, what is the current thought on this? Are there papers/texts that describe this in detail?

From a broad Lean/formalization point of view it seems that working as generally as possible has paid dividends in the long run because it's more flexible for future work and there have been cases where existing research didn't use the full generality but new research has made use of it and it was helpful to have the general version in Mathlib. I will also say that one application of Physlib (and formalization in general) is to determine what are the actual minimal assumptions needed for everything to work rather than formalizing everything literally as it exists now.

So just from the philosophy of what Physlib is trying to do I think it would make sense for us to be careful about discussing what should the core definitions be instead of what are they now. In that sense I think it's still worth chasing different perspectives and documenting their pros and cons for now as well as build out general math theory that may play a role.

But again, I'm not very knowledgeable about this so I could very well be off base.

Did I understand correctly that UnitalPositiveLinearMap is meant to correspond to a State? If this is in all cases maybe State would be a more physics appropriate name, or if it is only a State in some cases, maybe we should define an abbreviation for it in those cases.

I also see that @Tom Diem has opened Physlib#1607 and Physlib#1608 (many thanks for this!).

What should we do? Do we think it would be easy to join @David Gross's stuff with these PRs? Should we put some of this in PhyslibAlpha for the time being and then it could be upstreamed when we have settled on a foundation?

If that is okay with you @Tom Diem

My understanding of David’s proposal is that the main change is to introduce a smarter abstraction hierarchy. In my current approach, I’ve put essentially every notion into the OperatorAlgebra structure, whereas David is suggesting that concepts such as states should live at the most general level where they make mathematical sense, and that additional structure should only be introduced when a theorem actually requires it. For example, we should only specialize to C⋆-algebras or Hilbert-space operators when the result genuinely depends on that structure.

I think this makes a lot of sense, and I’m very much in favor of exploring this approach.

My impression is that the current QuantumInfo development has naturally been driven more by concrete results than by building this kind of general foundational layer, so I think David’s suggestion of developing the general theory separately in something like QuantumMechanics.Basic and only porting existing results incrementally if the approach proves successful is a good way forward.

Joseph Tooby-Smith schrieb:

I also see that @Tom Diem has opened Physlib#1607 and Physlib#1608 (many thanks for this!).

What should we do? Do we think it would be easy to join @David Gross's stuff with these PRs? Should we put some of this in PhyslibAlpha for the time being and then it could be upstreamed when we have settled on a foundation?

Sure, I’d be happy to move this into PhyslibAlpha. It would also let me iterate faster while the foundations are still being worked out, and having everything out in the open and in one place would probably make it easier for others to contribute.

I’m also not entirely sure what the downside would be of putting it directly into Physlib. At the moment very little depends on this code, and it could explicitly be treated as work in progress while we figure out the right abstractions. But I’m fine with either approach.

Regarding my current PRs: I don’t expect them to be the final form of these results, especially in light of David’s proposal. I still think they are useful for the discussion because they show what kind of physics we eventually want the foundational language to support. For example, a state together with an observable should give rise to a unique probability measure describing its measurement statistics, or Hamiltonian dynamics should satisfy a particular differential equation that follows from the underlying mathematical structure.

So I see these PRs partly as test cases for the abstraction layer: we can make the foundations more general, as David suggests, while checking that they still naturally recover the physics we actually care about.

I’m also not entirely sure what the downside would be of putting it directly into Physlib

Its more the review standards that go into it, I think. IMO it is best to keep the same standards of review throughout ./Physlib. This isn't to say that your PRs don't meet those standards, but to check whether they do takes a lot of time, especially for large PRs - so sometimes putting it in ./PhyslibAlpha makes more sense especially when we think they will change in the short-term.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Did I understand correctly that UnitalPositiveLinearMap is meant to correspond to a State?

UnitalPositiveLinearMap is the general mathematical concept that specializes to many things, including states of quantum / classical / post-quantum theories, or (not necessarily CP) channels, like time reversal and the partial transpose. It can also describes concepts that have no probabilistic interpretation at all.

If this is in all cases maybe State would be a more physics appropriate name, or if it is only a State in some cases, maybe we should define an abbreviation for it in those cases.

Yes. UnitalPositiveLinearMap is a mouthful. In the RFC, I've introduced some notation, like E₁ →ₚ₁[R] E₂ for general UPLMs, and 𝓢[E] for state space. A State abbrev would also work.

An alternative would be to teach users that 𝓐 →ₚ₁[ℂ] ℂ is how you say "state space of 𝓐" in Physlib and Mathlib. Like the Mathlib phrasebook. Avoiding physics jargon for concepts that make sense in math more broadly seems desirable, in order to reduce divergence between different libraries. ("State" is also used in math, but e.g. "channel" for a "cp map" less so).
Ok, I'm good with this. Though I think we should add something in the module-level documentation essentially along the lines of your comment here.

hi all, I'm trying to catch up with the latest developments here. Was there a conclusion on whether we would have fin-dim implementations at the foundational level for QM?

I've noticed operator algebras and GPTs being talked about here and this point interests me because operator algebras are very much dimension agnostic, whereas I have the impression GPTs are mostly developed for finite-dimensional systems, although I think they provide a more physically motivated basis for foundations (as opposed to mathematical, for operator algebras)

I think a level of implementations of both, and then a connection would be valuable, and maybe operator algebras would be more Physlib-oriented, and (today's) GPTs more QuantumInfo-oriented?

Hi Rodolfo,

I think this is the key question worth addressing as it's quite fundamental to the implementation problem.
I've built my repo on fin-dim at the foundational level which does work and I think it makes the problem solvable.

For context everything in my repo is finite dimensional and deliberately so. The main thing you get is that the completeness relation is a finite sum, so the weak topology question never arises, and a fair bit of the mathematical difficulty goes with it.

What's landed concretely: Naimark dilation generic over POVM N, Busch's Gleason type theorem proved rather than assumed, and the Born rule as a Fubini-Study volume via Duistermaat-Heckman at general N. It's Sorry free, with one posited sector I state openly.
See: https://github.com/zblore/csd-lean4

It's a foundations programme rather than a proposal for what Physlib should do though and your point about operator algebras being dimension agnostic is right. I just wouldn't assume fin-dim foundations are the lesser option, the constraints are different rather than weaker.

I agree with Daniel here. I think one way that we have handled this sort of thing in the past is with constructors. E.g. you have a single type e.g. QuantumOperator and define constructors for that operators in special cases (e.g. finite dimensional), e.g. QuantumOperator.ofMatrix. You can then define properties of these constructors. This is something we have done in Electromagnetism.

Rodolfo Soldati said:

I've noticed operator algebras and GPTs being talked about here and this point interests me because operator algebras are very much dimension agnostic, whereas I have the impression GPTs are mostly developed for finite-dimensional systems,

[Old guy putting his lecturer's hat on]

I don't think that historically accurate. What we call GPTs today was fully developed no later than the early 1980s (see e.g. Ludwig's monograph). There was certainly no assumption of finite dimensions in that tradition!

I guess the insight that interesting theory could be developed in finite-dimensional settings was popularized by Popescu-Rohrlic a decade later. (The Ludwig school would reply that Ludwig's PhD student Werner stated that result in a half-sentence much earlier -- search for "straightforward construction" in this paper. Bias disclosure: I used to work in Reinhard Werner's group). This seems to have started the quantum info-adjacent tradition of studying GPTs, which is indeed mostly finite-dimensional.

[end of lecture (sorry -- couldn't help it :upside_down: )]

In any case: I'm not advocating formalizing the general theory of GPTs for Physlib. All I'm doing is dropping unnecessary assumptions. I'm then just noting that what remains is general enough that it also encompasses states on operator algebras, GPTs, classical probability theory, and more.
